title: The missing middle in India's growth story
syllabus: GS3 › Growth, development and employment; Inclusive growth; Infrastructure; Energy · GS1 › Effects of globalisation; Social stratification
summary: India has stayed lower-middle income for 19 years while Vietnam and China moved up fast; five statistics show jobs, factories, private investment, power and a thin middle class holding it back.
evolution: India enters the World Bank's lower-middle-income group.
Vietnam, lower-middle income since 2009, moves up to upper-middle income this year: about 16 years.
China moves from lower-middle to upper-middle income in 13 years.
India still lower-middle income, 19 years on; five countries move up this year.
ideas: Stuck in the middle: India has been lower-middle income for 19 years; Vietnam and China moved up in 16 and 13. At 8.5% dollar growth, against 5.4% in the past decade, India could get there in about six years.
GS3 · Growth / middle-income trap
Nineteen years after turning lower-middle income, India is still there, while Vietnam took 16 years and China 13 to move up.

Jobs without productivity: the labour force grew by 100 million in under a decade, two-thirds of it women, mostly self-employed in farming; 43% still work in agriculture and 79% of non-farm workers are in informal firms.
GS3 employment · GS1 women
Employment is not productive employment: 43% of India's workers remain in agriculture and 79% of non-farm workers in informal enterprises.

Factories but no factory jobs: registered factories doubled, yet manufacturing's share of output and jobs has not risen; more workers joined the gig economy than formal manufacturing, and capital-intensive growth widened inequality.
GS3 · Manufacturing / inequality
Though registered factories doubled to 2.6 lakh, manufacturing has not become India's ladder of mass upward mobility.
Public investment has not crowded in private investment: infrastructure cut logistics costs, but firms repaired balance sheets and rewarded shareholders instead of investing.
GS3 · Investment
Public infrastructure spending was meant to crowd in private investment, but the private sector has not taken the baton.
Power is a binding constraint: solar has outrun storage and transmission, so output was curtailed even as demand peaked, hurting factories, data centres and AI.
GS3 · Energy / infrastructure
Solar generation running ahead of storage and transmission makes electricity a constraint on India's manufacturing and AI ambitions.
Rich faster than a middle class: 9.4 lakh dollar millionaires, but a broad middle class is not forming; premiumisation and capital outflows follow.
GS3 inclusive growth · GS1 inequality
India is producing millionaires faster than a broad middle class, the missing middle of its growth story.
keywords: Countries stuck at middle income, unable to move up
Without productive jobs, India risks a middle-income trap.
Workers moving from farms to factories and modern services
India's structural transformation has stalled: workers left farms for informal work, not factories.
Jobs with rising output and income per worker
Being employed is not the same as being productively employed.
Work that adds little output, taken because unemployment is unaffordable
The poor cannot afford to be unemployed, so low unemployment hides underemployment.
Public investment drawing in private investment
Public capex has not crowded in private investment.
Growth driven by machines more than labour
Capital-intensive manufacturing has raised profits faster than wages.
Premiumisation reflects growth concentrated at the top.
Women forming a growing share of farm work
Two-thirds of new workers are women, mostly self-employed in farming.
data: Rise in India's labour force in less than a decade; two-thirds women
India's labour force grew by over 100 million in under a decade, two-thirds of it women (World Bank).
Workforce still in agriculture / non-farm workers in informal enterprises
43% of India's workers are in agriculture, and 79% of non-farm workers are in informal enterprises.
Registered factories doubled from 1.3 lakh to 2.6 lakh, yet manufacturing's share stayed flat.
Dollar millionaires in India (alongside Switzerland, just behind Spain)
UBS Global Wealth Report, via IE
India has 9.4 lakh dollar millionaires (UBS), yet a thin middle class.
Dollar income growth needed vs achieved in the past decade to reach upper-middle income in about six years
At 8.5% dollar growth, against 5.4% recently, India could become upper-middle income in about six years.
examples: Lower-middle income in 2009; moved up to upper-middle income this year, about 16 years later
Vietnam moved from lower- to upper-middle income in 16 years, a model of manufacturing-led growth.
Upper-middle income in 2010, 13 years after becoming lower-middle
China reached upper-middle income in just 13 years by putting workers on factory floors.
Solar output cut despite peak demand, for lack of storage and transmission
In summer 2026, India curtailed solar power even at peak demand for lack of storage and grid.
pyqs: India skipped the manufacturing stage; the missing middle is the result.
Jobs grew with the labour force, but not productive jobs.
Manufacturing failed to become labour-intensive: factories doubled, factory jobs did not.
Industrial growth lagging GDP: manufacturing's share has not risen.
Growth led by more labour, not productivity: the 100 million new workers are mostly in low-value work.
Manufacturing's share in GDP and MSMEs: the core of the missing middle.
Infrastructure investment has cut logistics costs but not yet crowded in private investment.

trend.t: UPSC has asked the same structural question for a decade: India moved from agriculture to services and skipped manufacturing (2014), growth has been jobless (2015), manufacturing failed to become labour-intensive (2017) and growth rests on more labour, not productivity (2022). The latest questions ask for solutions: manufacturing and MSMEs (2023) and labour codes (2024).
trend.watch: Manufacturing and productive employment have come in 2014, 2017 (twice), 2022 and 2023. Structural transformation is a must-study area in GS3.
focus: Manufacturing-led jobs: PLI, MSMEs, labour-intensive sectors
Crowding in private investment after public capex
Power, storage and transmission as constraints on industry
Inequality and the middle class; women's productive employment

potential: India has remained a lower-middle-income country for nearly two decades. Discuss the structural constraints on its growth and suggest a strategy to create high-productivity jobs at scale. (15 marks)
Why has manufacturing not become the engine of employment in India despite the rise in registered factories? Examine. (10 marks)
Public investment in infrastructure has not crowded in private investment. Analyse the reasons and suggest measures. (10 marks)
India is producing millionaires faster than a broad middle class. Examine the implications for inclusive growth. (10 marks)

practice.q: India has remained a lower-middle-income country for nearly two decades. Discuss the structural constraints on its growth and suggest a strategy to create high-productivity jobs at scale.
parts: Introduction: India's 19 years at lower-middle income vs Vietnam and China (one line, with facts)
Strategy for high-productivity jobs (way forward, its own part)

answer.t: India has been lower-middle income since 2007, while Vietnam moved up in 16 years and China in 13 (World Bank).

pts.t: Workers moved from farms into informal work, not factories.
pts.ex: 43% still in agriculture; 79% of non-farm workers informal.

pts.t: Factories doubled, but manufacturing's share of output and jobs has not risen.
pts.ex: 1.3 lakh to 2.6 lakh registered factories, 2004-05 to 2024-25.

pts.t: Machines over labour keep wages behind profits and raise inequality.
Firms deleveraged and paid shareholders instead of building capacity, despite public capex.
Solar outruns storage and transmission, so supply is unreliable.
Two-thirds of new workers are women, mostly self-employed in agriculture.
Many workers lack skills for modern manufacturing and services.
Wealth concentrates at the top, limiting broad-based demand.
Prioritise textiles, apparel, footwear, electronics assembly and food processing.
Tie incentives to employment, not just output.
Predictable policy, faster clearances and demand certainty.
Storage, transmission and reliable, affordable supply.
Vocational training, childcare and safe transport to bring women into factories.
Flexibility for firms with social security for workers.

answer.t: India can escape the middle-income trap only by moving its workers from low- to high-productivity jobs, with public infrastructure and private capital working together.

title: To ease energy transition, ramp up storage, strengthen transmission
syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; Investment models; Conservation
context: A former CEA member writes that India has moved from chronic power deficits to a solar-hour glut and night-time deficits. The answer, he argues, is storage, stronger transmission, demand-side management and markets that reward flexibility.
ideas: Capacity is not the goal; power when people need it, by night as well as by day, is.
GS3 · Energy transition
India has moved from shortages to a solar-hour surplus, but night-time deficits show capacity is not enough.
Storage is the bottleneck: pumped storage is slow to build and bid prices are said to be unremunerative.
GS3 · Infrastructure
Storage is the bottleneck of India's energy transition; pumped storage is slow to build.
Wasted solar power and constant ramping of coal plants are a double loss.
GS3 · Resource efficiency
Curtailed solar and constant ramping of coal plants are a double loss for the grid.
keywords: Midday solar glut, evening demand peak
India's grid now faces a duck curve: a midday solar glut and an evening demand peak.
Clean power supplied at all hours
Storage and transmission are needed to deliver round-the-clock clean power.
Forcing generators to cut output the grid cannot absorb
Without storage, solar power is curtailed, wasting cheap clean energy.
Shifting or cutting demand to balance the grid
Demand-side management can shift use to solar hours and ease the evening peak.
data: Renewable capacity incl. large hydro, and its share of the total
Renewables, including large hydro, are about 292 GW, roughly 53% of India's installed capacity.
India's solar capacity has reached about 162 GW.
Thirty years ago 40% of Indians had no electricity (World Bank); today India has a daytime surplus.
pyqs: Capacity is not the only target: a solar-hour glut with night deficits shows storage and transmission are the bottleneck.
Grid flexibility and storage as part of energy security.
Cheap solar now forces coal plants to ramp up and down, shortening their life.
where: The Editorial Page, page 12 (Somit Dasgupta (teaser on page 1))
summary: India now has surplus power in solar hours and shortages at night; a former CEA member argues storage and transmission are the missing pieces.
evolution: 40% of Indians had no electricity (World Bank, cited in the article).
Electricity Act allowed state electricity boards to be split into separate companies.
Power exchanges in Delhi and Mumbai led to a capacity boom; over 1,00,000 MW of coal capacity added 2010-2020.
About 292 GW renewables (53% of capacity), 162 GW solar; daytime glut, night deficit.

title: Govt notifies E100 as auto fuel for flex-fuel vehicles
syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; Environment (pollution); Agriculture-linked industry
context: The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways amended the Central Motor Vehicle Rules to allow flex-fuel vehicles to run on up to E100 (nearly pure ethanol). Ordinary petrol or E20 vehicles cannot use E100.
ideas: Ethanol reduces dependence on imported crude oil.
GS3 · Energy security
Higher ethanol blends such as E100 cut India's dependence on imported crude.
Lower lifecycle emissions are possible, but they depend on the crop and the production process.
GS3 · Environment (balanced view)
Ethanol's climate benefit depends on the crop and process used, so lifecycle emissions must be counted.
keywords: Crops for ethanol compete with crops for food and water
Biofuel policy must manage the food-vs-fuel trade-off over land and water.
Vehicle built to run on different petrol-ethanol blends
Flex-fuel vehicles, now allowed to run on E100, offer a parallel route to cleaner transport alongside EVs.
Emissions across production, transport and use
Judged by lifecycle emissions, not tailpipe alone, biofuels are not automatically green.
Ethanol blending reduces import dependence and the oil import bill.
pyqs: Higher ethanol blends reduce dependence on imported crude.
Flex-fuel vehicles as a parallel route to cleaner transport alongside EVs.
links: Related Explained: Centre clears way for flex-fuel up to E100
summary: Flex-fuel vehicles may now run on E100, nearly pure ethanol; ordinary petrol and E20 vehicles cannot.
evolution: Ongoing debate over the use of E20 fuel (as the report notes).
E100 notified, but only for vehicles built as flex-fuel.
